Clinical Reference · Endocrine / Metabolic

Hypocalcemia

On this page
Albumin-corrected total calcium below 8.5 mg/dL (2.12 mmol/L) — or, better, ionized calcium below 1.16 mmol/L (4.65 mg/dL) — a spectrum running from an incidental number to tetany, laryngospasm, seizures, and a long-QT arrest. The single most useful next test is PTH: it splits the entire differential into "gland failed" vs "gland is fighting."
Neuromuscular irritability Severe: corrected Ca <7.5 mg/dL / ionized <0.8 mmol/L Long QT → torsades · laryngospasm · seizure Acute Rx: IV calcium gluconate + correct Mg Always check & replace magnesium
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

Calcium is the body's most tightly defended ion because it does two non-negotiable jobs: it stabilizes excitable membranes (nerve and muscle) and it triggers contraction, secretion, and clotting. Only the ionized (free) fraction — about 50% of total calcium — is biologically active. Roughly 40% is bound to albumin and 10% is complexed to anions (citrate, phosphate, bicarbonate). That is why a low total calcium in a hypoalbuminemic patient may hide a perfectly normal ionized calcium — a "pseudohypocalcemia" that needs no treatment.

Three hormones defend the set-point. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is the minute-to-minute thermostat: the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on the parathyroid chief cell reads the free calcium; when it falls, PTH is released within seconds. PTH raises calcium by three levers — it resorbs bone (osteoclast activation releases calcium and phosphate), it makes the kidney reabsorb calcium in the distal tubule while dumping phosphate, and it switches on renal 1α-hydroxylase, converting 25-OH vitamin D into active calcitriol (1,25-OH₂ D), which then drives gut absorption of calcium and phosphate. Hypocalcemia results whenever this axis is broken at any node: the gland fails (hypoparathyroidism), the gland is resisted (pseudohypoparathyroidism, hypomagnesemia), the vitamin D arm is empty (deficiency, CKD), calcium is chelated or precipitated (citrate, phosphate, pancreatitis), or bone gulps it back (hungry bone, osteoblastic metastases).

Think of ionized calcium as the voltage stabilizer sitting on every nerve and muscle "power line." Calcium ions plug the sodium channels' outer gate, so it takes a real stimulus to fire. Drop the calcium and you pull the stabilizers off the line — the channels leak, neurons fire on their own, and you get the sparking short-circuits of tetany: tingling, cramps, carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, seizures. PTH and vitamin D are the two utility crews that keep the line charged: PTH the fast responder (pulls calcium from the bone "warehouse" and the kidney "recycling plant" in seconds), vitamin D the slow supply chain (opens the gut "loading dock" over hours to days).
The calcium thermostat: PTH + calcitriol raise serum calcium through bone, kidney, and gut. Each therapy in this guide re-supplies one of these columns.
Integrated calcium homeostasis — PTH, calcitriol and calcitonin feedback on bone, kidney and gut.

The four parathyroid glands behind the thyroid — the CaSR-driven PTH source, and the structures at risk during thyroid/neck surgery.
CFCF, Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
Calcitriol (1,25-OH₂ vitamin D) — the active hormone. Giving it directly bypasses the failed renal 1α-hydroxylase step in hypoparathyroidism and CKD.
NEUROtiker, Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
Ionized calcium plugs the voltage sensor of neuronal Na⁺ channels. Remove it and the firing threshold falls toward resting potential, so nerves discharge on their own — paresthesias, cramps, carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, seizures, and QT prolongation.
Every therapy in this guide re-supplies one broken column of the diagram above. IV/oral calcium = refill the pool directly. Calcitriol / active vitamin D = restart the gut "loading dock" (and bypass the failed renal 1α-hydroxylase in hypoparathyroidism and CKD). Ergo-/cholecalciferol = refill the 25-OH substrate when the deficiency is nutritional. Magnesium = re-enable PTH secretion and action (low Mg jams both). Thiazide + low-sodium diet = make the kidney hold calcium (used in hypoparathyroidism, where there is no PTH to do it). Recombinant PTH / palopegteriparatide = replace the missing hormone itself. Phosphate binders = stop phosphate from precipitating calcium out of solution.
🗂️

Classification — split by PTH, then by phosphate

The whole differential collapses onto one measurement — PTH — then a second — phosphate. A low/inappropriately-normal PTH means the gland is the problem; a high PTH means the gland is working and the problem is elsewhere (and phosphate then tells you which "elsewhere").

PTHCategoryPhosphateRepresentative causes
Low / inappropriately normalPTH-dependent (hypoparathyroidism)High (no PTH to waste it)Post-surgical (thyroid/parathyroid/neck) — most common; autoimmune / APS-1; genetic (DiGeorge 22q11, ADH/CaSR-activating); infiltration (Wilson, hemochromatosis, metastasis); radiation; hypomagnesemia (functional)
High (appropriate)PTH-independent, high phosphateHighCKD (low calcitriol + phosphate retention); tumor lysis syndrome; rhabdomyolysis; acute phosphate load / enemas
High (appropriate)PTH-independent, low/normal phosphateLow / normalVitamin D deficiency; malabsorption / post-bariatric; acute pancreatitis (saponification); osteoblastic metastases; "hungry bone" post-parathyroidectomy
High + resistancePseudohypoparathyroidismHighEnd-organ PTH resistance (GNAS defect) — high PTH but it doesn't work; Albright hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype

Severity — what the number means and how fast to move

BandCorrected total CaIonized CaTypical picture & tempo
Mild8.0–8.4 mg/dL (2.0–2.1 mmol/L)1.03–1.15 mmol/LOften asymptomatic; outpatient work-up & oral repletion
Moderate7.5–7.9 mg/dL (1.9–2.0 mmol/L)0.9–1.03 mmol/LParesthesias, cramps, Chvostek/Trousseau; treat, look for the driver
Severe / emergency<7.5 mg/dL (<1.9 mmol/L)<0.8 mmol/LTetany, laryngospasm, seizures, long QT / arrhythmia, altered mental status → IV calcium now, regardless of the exact number if symptomatic
Symptoms track the rate of fall as much as the absolute value. A chronic hypoparathyroid patient can walk around at 6.5 mg/dL, while a brisk post-op drop to 7.5 mg/dL can seize. Treat the patient and the trajectory, not just the lab.

Comorbidities & drug cautions

🔗

How common comorbidities change the disease — and the plan

ComorbidityHow it changes the courseHow it changes management
CKD / dialysisLow calcitriol + phosphate retention → chronic hypocalcemia with high PTH; prototypical secondary hyperparathyroidismUse active vitamin D (calcitriol) — the failed 1α-hydroxylase is bypassed; control phosphate; avoid raising Ca×PO₄; correct Ca/vit D before any antiresorptive
Post-thyroid / parathyroid surgeryCommonest cause overall — transient ~25% (up to 49%), permanent ~1–5%; nadir day 2–4; hungry-bone riskPost-op PTH at 4–6 h predicts need; prophylactic calcium ± calcitriol; watch the day 2–4 dip
Vitamin D deficiency / malabsorption / bariatricEmpties the gut-absorption arm → high-PTH hypocalcemiaReplete D (higher doses; parenteral if malabsorption); prefer calcium citrate (acid-independent) after bypass/on PPI
Acute pancreatitisSaponification chelates calcium; hypocalcemia is a severity marker (Ranson)Treat symptomatic hypocalcemia; expect it to track disease course — don't over-correct
Tumor lysis / rhabdomyolysisHyperphosphatemia precipitates calcium-phosphateDo NOT chase calcium up while phosphate is high (metastatic calcification); fix phosphate; calcium only for symptomatic/severe
Heart failure / QT-prolonging drugsHypocalcemia lengthens QT (additive) and can cause a reversible cardiomyopathyCorrect calcium (may reverse the cardiomyopathy); avoid stacking QT-prolongers; monitor QTc
Chronic PPI useCauses hypomagnesemia (→ functional hypoparathyroidism) and blunts calcium-carbonate absorptionCheck & replace Mg; switch to calcium citrate; reconsider PPI necessity
Pregnancy / lactationCalcium and calcitriol demands shift substantially in hypoparathyroidismEndocrine co-management; frequent monitoring and dose adjustment
Sepsis / critical illnessMultifactorial ionized hypocalcemia, tracks severity/mortalityTreat symptomatic/severe; routine correction of asymptomatic ionized hypocalcemia is unproven
Drugs to avoid / use with caution in hypocalcemia:
  • Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide) — increase urinary calcium loss and worsen hypocalcemia. Common misconception: loops treat hypercalcemia, not hypo. In hypoparathyroidism the opposite drug — a thiazide — is used to retain calcium.
  • Denosumab & IV bisphosphonates (zoledronate) — can precipitate severe, prolonged hypocalcemia, especially with vitamin D deficiency or CKD. FDA boxed warning (Jan 2024): denosumab causes severe hypocalcemia in ~41% of dialysis patients — correct calcium/vitamin D first and monitor at weeks 2–5.
  • Foscarnet — directly chelates ionized calcium (acute drop with a normal total).
  • Cinacalcet / calcimimetics — activate the CaSR → suppress PTH → lower calcium.
  • Phenytoin / phenobarbital — induce hepatic catabolism of vitamin D.
  • Phosphate loads / phosphate enemas and citrate (massive transfusion, CRRT) — precipitate or chelate calcium.
  • QT-prolonging antiarrhythmics — additive torsades risk with hypocalcemic long QT.
  • Sodium bicarbonate — alkalosis lowers ionized calcium and it precipitates with calcium in the same IV line.

Clinical pearls

💡

The dozen things that change management at the bedside

  1. Order an ionized calcium for any real decision. Total calcium is distorted by albumin, pH, and gadolinium — and the Payne "correction" can be less accurate than the uncorrected total against a measured ionized level.
  2. Check and replace magnesium first. Low Mg causes functional hypoparathyroidism (blocks PTH secretion and action) — calcium will not correct until Mg is repleted.
  3. PTH is the fork in the road. Low/normal PTH + high phosphate = hypoparathyroidism; high PTH = CKD, vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption, or PTH resistance.
  4. Units: for calcium, 1 mmol/L = 4 mg/dL, and (divalent) 1 mmol/L = 2 mEq/L. Sources mix units constantly — convert deliberately.
  5. Calcium chloride ≈ 3× the elemental calcium of gluconate per gram (273 vs ~90 mg) but is a vesicant → central line. Gluconate is the peripheral workhorse.
  6. A bolus wears off in 2–3 h. Follow severe/symptomatic hypocalcemia with a continuous infusion at 0.5–1.5 mg elemental Ca/kg/h.
  7. Trousseau (≈94% sens/99% spec) beats Chvostek (positive in 10–25% of normal people; negative in ~30% of true hypocalcemics).
  8. Alkalosis/hyperventilation causes symptomatic ionized hypocalcemia with a normal total calcium (~5% ionized change per 0.1 pH unit).
  9. Denosumab in advanced CKD is dangerous — FDA boxed warning (2024); correct calcium/vitamin D first and monitor weeks 2–5.
  10. Suspect gadolinium pseudohypocalcemia in profound, asymptomatic hypocalcemia right after a contrast MRI (esp. gadodiamide) — re-run by a different assay.
  11. Don't chase calcium up in tumor lysis/hyperphosphatemia — risk of metastatic calcification; fix the phosphate and treat only symptomatic hypocalcemia.
  12. In chronic hypoparathyroidism aim for low-normal calcium and keep 24-h urine Ca <250 mg (women)/<300 mg (men) to protect the kidneys.
  13. The digoxin "stone heart" ban is largely myth — give calcium (slowly) when it is genuinely needed; and remember hypocalcemia can cause a reversible cardiomyopathy and a long QT.
🩺 Clinic — outpatient work-up & chronic management
Assess

When to suspect

🔍

Outpatient presentation & who is at risk

Chronic, mild hypocalcemia is frequently asymptomatic and found on a routine metabolic panel — the highest-yield move is to correct the total calcium for albumin before you believe it. Symptoms, when present, are those of neuromuscular irritability and track the rate of the fall. Highest-risk outpatients: prior thyroid/parathyroid/neck surgery, CKD, malabsorption / bariatric surgery, chronic PPI use, alcohol use, and anyone on denosumab or a bisphosphonate (especially with low vitamin D or low eGFR).

Symptom / sign~Frequency*Why it happens
Perioral & fingertip/toe paresthesias~50%Earliest symptom; sensory-nerve membranes depolarize spontaneously once Ca²⁺ stops shielding Na⁺ channels
Muscle cramps, spasms, "twitchiness"~45%Motor-nerve & muscle hyperexcitability (same channel mechanism)
Trousseau sign (carpopedal spasm on BP-cuff inflation 3 min)~94% sensCuff ischemia + pressure unmasks latent tetany; more sensitive/specific than Chvostek
Fatigue, generalized weakness~40%Impaired excitation–contraction & cardiac output at low ionized Ca²⁺
Prolonged QTc on ECG~30%Low Ca²⁺ lengthens the plateau (phase 2) of the action potential → long ST/QT
Chvostek sign (facial twitch on tapping CN VII)~25% sensFacial-nerve hyperexcitability — but present in ~10–25% of normocalcemic people, so low specificity
Anxiety, irritability, depressed mood (chronic)~20%CNS neuronal irritability; chronic hypoparathyroidism affects mood/cognition
Frank tetany / spontaneous carpopedal spasm~15%Severe/rapid drop; sustained involuntary contraction ("main d'accoucheur")
Seizure (focal or generalized)~10%Cortical neuronal hyperexcitability; can occur with a normal EEG background
Cataracts / posterior subcapsular (chronic)~10%Chronic hypocalcemia disturbs lens Ca²⁺ homeostasis → opacification
Laryngospasm / bronchospasm / stridor<5%Tetany of laryngeal muscles — rare but immediately life-threatening
Basal-ganglia calcification (Fahr), movement disorder, dementia, papilledema, enamel/nail/skin changeschronicLong-standing hypoparathyroidism: metastatic calcification (high Ca×PO₄ product) & ectodermal effects; often an incidental CT finding

*Approximate frequencies among symptomatic hypocalcemia; Trousseau/Chvostek values are elicited-test sensitivities, not spontaneous-presentation rates. Color: red >70% · amber 40–70% · blue 15–40% · purple <15%.

What to order & when

🧪

Labs & imaging — and the order they change decisions

Ionized calciumWhen albumin is abnormal, in acid–base disturbance, critical illness, citrate exposure, or to confirm true hypocalcemia. The gold standard — measures the active fraction directly.Confirm

The one algorithm to memorize — split by PTH, then phosphate

PTH-first diagnostic algorithm for confirmed hypocalcemia. Draw PTH and calcium together; check magnesium in every low-PTH case.

How to read each abnormal lab (and what moves it falsely)

LabWhat it means hereFalsely raised / lowered by
Total calciumScreen; must be albumin-correctedFalsely LOW with hypoalbuminemia (nephrotic, cirrhosis, malnutrition); some gadolinium contrast agents spuriously lower colorimetric Ca assays
Ionized calciumThe true active fraction — gold standardFalls with alkalosis (↑ albumin binding; hyperventilation can trigger tetany) and with citrate/EDTA; rises with acidosis and prolonged tourniquet
PTHLow/normal = gland failure; high = secondary/appropriateInterpret ONLY alongside a simultaneous calcium — "normal" PTH with low Ca is inappropriately normal = hypoparathyroidism
PhosphateHigh with hypopara/CKD/TLS; low with vitamin D deficiencyHemolysis and delayed spin falsely raise it; recent meal/insulin lowers it
MagnesiumLow Mg → functional hypoparathyroidismSerum Mg underestimates total-body depletion (mostly intracellular) — replace even if "low-normal"
Alkaline phosphataseHigh in vitamin D-deficiency osteomalacia & hungry-bone syndrome (bone turnover)Low in hypophosphatasia; raised by pregnancy/growth/cholestasis (check GGT)

Corrected calcium calculator (Payne formula)

Corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin g/dL). Use when albumin is abnormal; when in doubt, order an ionized calcium.

—

Formula source: Payne RB et al., BMJ 1973. Each 1 g/dL fall in albumin below 4.0 hides ~0.8 mg/dL of calcium.

Treat

Chronic management

💊

Stepwise therapy — first-line → escalation

Fix the cause first. Nutritional vitamin D deficiency → replace D. Low magnesium → replace Mg (calcium won't budge otherwise). CKD → active vitamin D + phosphate control. Hypoparathyroidism → the lifelong calcium + active-vitamin-D (± thiazide ± PTH) regimen below. Target corrected Ca in the low-normal range (≈8.0–8.5 mg/dL) — deliberately low, to avoid hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis in patients who have no PTH to protect the kidney.
1
First-line — oral calcium + active vitamin D
The backbone of chronic hypoparathyroidism and most repletion.
▾
Oral calcium refills the pool; calcitriol restarts gut absorption and bypasses the failed renal 1α-hydroxylase step — which is exactly what's missing in hypoparathyroidism and CKD. Plain vitamin D (chole-/ergocalciferol) refills the substrate when the deficiency is nutritional.
DrugStartTitrationTarget / MaxWhy / monitorIf intolerant / alt
Calcium carbonate (40% elemental)500 mg elemental BID with meals↑ by 500 mg/day every 1–2 wk1–3 g elemental/day divided (max ~3 g)Cheapest, densest; needs gastric acid → take with foodCalcium citrate if on PPI / post-bariatric / constipated
Calcium citrate (21% elemental)200–400 mg elemental BID–TID↑ per calcium level1–2 g elemental/day dividedAbsorbed without acid; fewer GI/stone issuesCalcium carbonate if pill burden a problem (more elemental/pill)
Calcitriol (1,25-OH₂ D)0.25 mcg daily (or BID)↑ by 0.25 mcg every 4–7 days0.5–2 mcg/day (occasionally higher)Active hormone — fast on/off; monitor Ca, phosphate, urine CaAlfacalcidol where available; avoid overshoot → hypercalciuria
Cholecalciferol (D₃) / ergocalciferol (D₂)Deficiency: 50,000 IU weekly ×6–8 wkthen maintenanceMaintenance 800–2000 IU/day; keep 25-OH D >30 ng/mLReplenishes 25-OH substrate; corrects the commonest PTH-independent causeD₂ (ergocalciferol) is vegan-suitable

Elemental content cheat-sheet: carbonate 40% · citrate 21% · gluconate 9% · lactate 13% · chloride 27%. "1 g calcium carbonate" ≈ 400 mg elemental calcium.

2
If hypercalciuria / inadequate control — add a thiazide, control phosphate, fix Mg
Reduce urinary calcium loss; protect the kidney.
▾
In hypoparathyroidism there is no PTH to reabsorb calcium in the distal nephron, so calcium spills into urine (nephrocalcinosis, stones). A thiazide + low-sodium diet enhances proximal calcium reabsorption and lowers urine calcium.

Hydrochlorothiazide12.5–25 mg daily + low-Na⁺ diet↑ toward 25 mg BID~50 mg/day (divided)Cuts urinary calcium; watch for hypokalemia & hyponatremiaChlorthalidone (longer-acting); add K⁺-sparing if hypokalemic
Magnesium (oral)Mg oxide 400 mg daily (if low)↑ to BID as toleratedNormalize serum Mg; diarrhea limits doseRestores PTH secretion/action — a common reversible causeMg glycinate/lactate (better tolerated); IV if severe/symptomatic

Refractory — PTH replacement & endocrine referral
When calcium + active vitamin D can't achieve control (or doses cause hypercalciuria).
▾
The most physiologic fix for hypoparathyroidism is to replace the missing hormone itself, restoring renal calcium handling and calcitriol production and cutting pill burden.

Monitor

Titration & follow-up

📈

What to recheck, and when

PhaseCheckCadenceGoal
Active titrationCorrected/ionized Ca, phosphate, Mg, creatinineEvery 1–2 weeks until stableCorrected Ca 8.0–8.5 mg/dL; relieve symptoms without overshoot
Stable, establishedCa, phosphate, creatinine, MgEvery 3–6 months, then 6–12 monthsLow-normal Ca; avoid hyperphosphatemia
Annual surveillance24-h urine calcium; renal ultrasound; slit-lamp; eGFRYearlyUrine Ca <300 mg/24 h; detect nephrocalcinosis/cataract early
The goal is deliberately low-normal. Chasing a "normal" 9.5 mg/dL in a hypoparathyroid patient floods the urine with calcium (no PTH to reclaim it) and scars the kidneys. If urine calcium climbs, add a thiazide before pushing calcium/calcitriol higher.
Nephrocalcinosis — the price of over-treatment. With no PTH to reabsorb filtered calcium, aggressive repletion drives hypercalciuria, stones, and nephrocalcinosis. Keep 24-h urine Ca <250 mg (women) / <300 mg (men).

Prevent

USPSTF & prevention

🛡️

The honest USPSTF picture for calcium/vitamin D

Hypocalcemia itself is not a USPSTF screening topic — there is no Grade A/B recommendation to screen asymptomatic adults for it. The closest, and most-misquoted, touchpoints are about vitamin D and calcium supplementation:

GradeRecommendation (year)Population
IScreening asymptomatic adults for vitamin D deficiency — insufficient evidence (2021)Community-dwelling, non-pregnant adults
DAgainst daily low-dose vitamin D (≤400 IU) + calcium (≤1000 mg) for primary fracture prevention (2018)Community-dwelling postmenopausal women
IHigher-dose D + calcium for fracture prevention — insufficient evidence (2018)Men & premenopausal women
BExercise interventions to prevent falls (2018)Community-dwelling adults ≥65 at increased fall risk

Takeaway: don't reflexively "screen" for vitamin D, and don't use low-dose calcium/D for primary prevention in average-risk postmenopausal women. This is different from treating documented deficiency or hypoparathyroidism, which is indicated.

Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Send to the ED for IV calcium if any of: seizure, tetany, laryngospasm/stridor, carpopedal spasm; corrected Ca <7.5 mg/dL (or ionized <0.8 mmol/L) even if "only" mildly symptomatic; prolonged QTc, syncope, or any arrhythmia; new severe symptoms after recent thyroid/parathyroid/neck surgery; or a symptomatic drop after denosumab/bisphosphonate.
Give the patient a written "sick-day" plan: if tingling/spasms worsen, take an extra calcium dose and seek care. Denosumab recipients with CKD or low vitamin D are the classic outpatients who crash to a dangerous level 1–2 weeks after the injection.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient repletion
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & initial profile

Admit anyone who needs IV calcium, cardiac monitoring, or serial labs faster than clinic allows. The decision is driven by symptoms, the corrected/ionized level, the QT, and the trajectory — not the number alone.

  • Any severe symptom — tetany, seizure, laryngospasm/stridor, carpopedal spasm, or an arrhythmia.
  • Corrected Ca <7.5 mg/dL (ionized <0.9 mmol/L) even if only mildly symptomatic, or a rapid drop.
  • Prolonged QTc on ECG.
  • Post-thyroidectomy / parathyroidectomy symptomatic hypocalcemia, or suspected hungry bone syndrome.
  • Denosumab- or bisphosphonate-induced severe hypocalcemia (especially with CKD).
  • Unable to take or absorb oral calcium; needs IV repletion.
Post-thyroidectomy calcium nadirs at day 2–4 — a patient discharged "normal" on day 1 can crash at home. Many centers use a postoperative PTH at 4–6 h to predict who will need calcium/calcitriol.

Treat

Acute management

💊

Stepwise inpatient therapy — bolus → drip → oral bridge

Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia pathway. A bolus buys ~2–3 hours; anyone truly hypocalcemic needs a continuous infusion and an early oral bridge. (Doses: PMC3474611 endocrine-emergencies review; StatPearls.)
1
IV bolus — symptomatic, Ca <7.5, or long QT
Stabilize the membrane now; fix Mg at the same time.
▾
IV calcium immediately re-shields the sodium channels and shortens the QT. It wears off in ~2–3 h, so it is a bridge to the drip and oral therapy — not a cure.
AgentStart (bolus)Repeat / titrateRoute / maxWhy / monitorAlt
Calcium gluconate 10%1–2 g (10–20 mL = 90–180 mg elemental) in 50–100 mL D5W over 10–20 minRepeat q10–60 min until symptoms resolvePeripheral OK; cardiac monitorWorkhorse; lower osmolarity → peripheral-safeCalcium chloride 1 g if central access & need more elemental fast
Magnesium sulfate2 g (8 mmol) IV over 10–20 min if Mg lowthen 4 g over ~4 h PRNConcurrent with calciumCalcium won't correct until Mg is replacedOral Mg if mild & asymptomatic
2
Continuous calcium infusion ("calcium drip")
For severe or persistent hypocalcemia after the bolus.
▾
Sustains the level between boluses. Titrate to a low-normal calcium — over-correction causes hypercalciuria and, with high phosphate, metastatic calcification.
PrepStartTitrateTargetMonitorNote
100 mL of 10% Ca gluconate (~10 g ≈ 900 mg elemental) in 1 L D5W/NS ≈ 1 mg/mL elemental50–100 mL/hAdjust to deliver 0.5–1.5 mg elemental Ca/kg/hCorrected Ca ~8.0–8.5 mg/dL (ionized ~1.0–1.1)Recheck Ca q4–6h; watch phosphate, Mg, IV siteAvoid mixing calcium with bicarbonate/phosphate lines (precipitates)
3
Oral bridge & wean; hungry-bone doses
Start oral early; the drip is a bridge.
▾

Start oral calcium 1–2 g elemental/day divided + calcitriol 0.25–0.5 mcg BID as soon as the gut works, then wean the drip once the oral regimen holds the calcium. Correct the underlying cause (vitamin D, CKD, the offending drug).

Hungry bone syndrome (post-parathyroidectomy for severe HPT) is voracious: it can need 6–12 g/day elemental calcium (occasionally more) plus calcitriol 2–4 mcg/day, with q4–6h calcium checks and aggressive Mg/phosphate replacement until the skeleton is satisfied.
IV calcium salt. Gluconate is the peripheral workhorse; calcium chloride carries ~3× the elemental calcium per gram but is a vesicant needing a central line.
User:Walkerma, Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
Hypocalcemia lengthens the ST segment → a long QT. Trend the QTc; a long QT is the trigger for telemetry and faster repletion.
Mikael Häggström, Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • Calcium — ionized/corrected q4–6h during a drip (FDA label: q1–4h), spacing to daily once stable and rising.
  • Magnesium & phosphate daily — low Mg stalls correction; rising phosphate limits how hard you can push calcium.
  • ECG / QTc until normalized; keep telemetry while severe.
  • Symptoms & exam — resolution of paresthesias, Chvostek/Trousseau; IV-site checks for extravasation.
  • Oral transition — confirm the calcium holds off the drip for ≥24 h before discharge.

Corrected QT (QTc, Bazett) calculator

Hypocalcemia lengthens the ST/QT — trend the QTc. QTc = QT ÷ √(RR), where RR = 60 ÷ heart rate.

—

Bazett over-corrects at high rates and under-corrects at low rates. Flags: prolonged >450 ms (men) / >470 ms (women); high torsades risk >500 ms. Source: MDCalc Corrected QT (Bazett).

Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers

Transfer to ICU for any of: seizure, laryngospasm, or airway compromise; ventricular arrhythmia / torsades or refractory QTc prolongation; hemodynamic instability / hypotension or heart failure not responding until calcium is corrected; need for a central line + high-rate continuous calcium infusion with continuous telemetry; ionized Ca <0.8 mmol/L with instability (<0.65 is critically low); or a driver needing intensive management — massive transfusion / citrate toxicity, tumor lysis, severe pancreatitis.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: calcium stable and rising on an oral regimen for ≥24 h off IV; symptoms resolved; QTc normalized; the cause identified and addressed (vitamin D started, offending drug stopped, endocrine follow-up for hypoparathyroidism); a follow-up calcium check and clinic visit scheduled; patient taught the sick-day plan.

Home

Stable on oral calcium + calcitriol; reliable, can fill scripts, has a recheck booked.

Home health

Needs nursing for lab draws / injection teaching (e.g., new PTH-replacement) or frail but home-safe.

SNF

Needs 24-h skilled monitoring/repletion but not ICU-level; post-op complex cases.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Rarely driven by hypocalcemia itself; if a seizure/fall caused deconditioning needing ≥3 h therapy/day.

LTAC

Uncommon; only if a prolonged critical-illness course (e.g., citrate-dependent CRRT).

Hospice / palliative

When hypocalcemia is a marker of end-stage malignancy and goals are comfort-focused.
🫀 ICU — critical care, citrate circuits & refractory repletion
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

Ionized hypocalcemia is nearly ubiquitous in the ICU (≈55–88%) and tracks with severity and mortality — but routinely correcting asymptomatic ionized hypocalcemia has not been shown to improve outcomes. Treat the symptomatic, the severe, and the citrate-driven; don't chase an incidental number in a stable patient.

ICU-level hypocalcemia = any of: seizure, laryngospasm / airway compromise, ventricular arrhythmia / torsades or refractory long QT, hypotension or heart failure that stays refractory until calcium is corrected, ionized Ca <0.8 mmol/L with instability (<0.65 = critically low), or citrate toxicity (massive transfusion, CRRT with regional citrate, apheresis) / tumor lysis needing intensive management.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

Ionized calciumThe ICU decision variable — q2–4h during active repletion or citrate circuits. Do NOT trust total calcium here (citrate makes total normal/high while ionized falls).q2–4h
Central venous accessRequired for calcium chloride or a prolonged high-rate infusion (vesicant → necrosis on extravasation).Access
Arterial line + telemetryFrequent iCa sampling & beat-to-beat pressure; continuous telemetry with QTc trending.Continuous
Mg, phosphate, pH/ABGMg to unblock correction; phosphate to gate how hard you push calcium; alkalosis lowers ionized Ca (~5% per 0.1 pH) — hyperventilation alone can trigger tetany.Serial
Support

IV calcium & hemodynamics

💉

Which calcium salt, the infusion, and calcium as an inotrope

AgentElemental content / osmolarityDoseEffectWhen to pick
Calcium gluconate 10%~90 mg elemental/g (10 mL = 1 g); ~670 mOsm/LBolus 1–2 g over 10–20 min; infusion 0.5–1.5 mg/kg/h elementalRestores membrane stability & contractilityDefault; peripheral-safe
Calcium chloride 10%~273 mg elemental/g (~3×); ~2040 mOsm/L (vesicant)0.5–1 g over 10–20 min via central lineFaster, denser elemental loadPeri-arrest / rapid rise with central access
Magnesium sulfateCo-factor for PTH2 g IV over 10–20 min, then 4 g/4 h PRNUnblocks PTH secretion/actionAny low/low-normal Mg (do first)
Calcium is a direct positive inotrope — cytosolic Ca²⁺ drives excitation–contraction coupling. Severe ionized hypocalcemia can cause hypotension and reduced contractility that stay refractory to catecholamine pressors until the calcium is corrected. In pressor-resistant shock, check an ionized calcium and replace it; calcium is an adjunct to — not a replacement for — norepinephrine.
Never run calcium in the same line as sodium bicarbonate or phosphate — they precipitate as calcium carbonate/phosphate. Flush or use a separate lumen.
Circuits

Citrate: transfusion, CRRT & apheresis

🧊

The ICU-specific cause you must recognize

Citrate chelates ionized calcium. The tell-tale pattern is a normal or high total calcium with a low ionized calcium, because the citrate-bound calcium is still counted in the total. The liver normally clears the ~3 g of citrate in a unit of blood within minutes, but shock, hepatic dysfunction, hypothermia, and acidemia slow clearance and let citrate accumulate.

SettingMechanismManagement
Massive transfusion~3 g citrate/unit PRBC binds iCa faster than the liver clears itMonitor ionized Ca; give calcium gluconate/chloride per protocol during rapid transfusion
CRRT — regional citrate anticoagulationCitrate deliberately lowers iCa in the circuit; systemic calcium is reinfusedTitrate calcium reinfusion to systemic iCa; watch for citrate accumulation (rising total:ionized ratio, metabolic acidosis, worsening iCa)
Apheresis / plasma exchangeCitrate anticoagulant in the extracorporeal circuitPerioral tingling is the early sign; prophylactic/PRN calcium
In any citrate circuit, follow the ionized calcium and the total:ionized ratio — a rising ratio (>~2.5) signals citrate accumulation, not simple hypocalcemia, and the fix is to reduce citrate load, not just pour in more calcium.
Rescue

Refractory & "do not over-correct"

⚙️

When calcium won't rise — and when NOT to push it

Refractory hypocalcemia — work the checklist

  • Is magnesium replaced? The commonest reason calcium won't correct. Recheck and re-dose.
  • Ongoing chelation/precipitation? Citrate still running, or a high phosphate precipitating calcium — address the source.
  • Is calcitriol on board? Without active vitamin D, oral/IV calcium under-performs in hypoparathyroidism and CKD.
  • Escalate the infusion and consider central calcium chloride if peripheral gluconate can't keep up.

When NOT to reflexively give calcium

Tumor lysis / hyperphosphatemia: raising calcium while phosphate is high risks metastatic calcification (Ca×PO₄ >~60). Fix the phosphate; give calcium only for symptomatic/severe hypocalcemia. Asymptomatic ICU ionized hypocalcemia: routine correction is unproven and debated — reserve treatment for symptomatic or severe (ionized <~0.8) cases.
Digoxin "stone heart" is largely a myth. The old teaching to withhold IV calcium in digoxin toxicity is not supported by modern data (a retrospective cohort found no excess mortality or early arrhythmia). Give calcium when it is genuinely needed — ideally slowly — rather than withholding it from a tetanic or arresting patient.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when: off the continuous calcium infusion with ionized Ca stable ≥0.9–1.0 mmol/L on an oral (or low-rate) regimen; symptoms resolved; QTc normalized and no arrhythmia for ≥24 h; the citrate source resolved (transfusion finished, CRRT stable per protocol); Mg and phosphate controlled.
Not yet if: still requiring a high-rate calcium drip, QT still prolonged, active torsades risk, ongoing citrate accumulation on CRRT, or an unresolved high-turnover state (tumor lysis, hungry bone) still consuming grams of calcium per day.

Sources, trials & guidelines

🧪

Landmark trials & practice-changing evidence

Trial / sourceYearResultWhy it matters
REPLACE (Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol, phase 3, n=124)2013rhPTH(1-84) 50→75→100 µg/day met the 3-tier endpoint in 54.8% vs 2.5% placebo; large cuts in oral calcium/calcitriolFirst proof that replacing the hormone works in hypoparathyroidism — opened PTH-replacement therapy
PaTHway / palopegteriparatide (TransCon PTH)2023–24Long-acting PTH prodrug normalized calcium and eliminated conventional therapy in most; FDA-approved (YORVIPATH) for adult hypoparathyroidismThe current, physiologic option when conventional Ca + calcitriol fails or over-treats
FDA Drug Safety Communication — denosumab in advanced CKD2024Severe hypocalcemia in 41.1% vs 2.0% (dialysis), very-severe 10.9% vs 0.4%; nadir weeks 2–5 → boxed warningCorrect calcium/vitamin D before antiresorptives in CKD; a leading iatrogenic cause
Calcium correction vs ionized (JAMA Network, n=22,658)—Uncorrected total Ca matched ionized status 74.5% vs ~63% for the Payne correction — correction was worseOrder an ionized calcium for real decisions; don't trust the corrected number
IV calcium in digoxin toxicity (retrospective cohort)—23/161 toxic patients given calcium: no excess mortality, no early arrhythmiaThe "stone heart" ban is largely myth — give calcium when truly indicated
